source: Marqu - The Hebrew Gospel of Mark v1.2

verses.translation: And they came{H935} across{H5676} to the sea{H3220} opposite{H5048} Ginnesaret.

one_way_hebrew: Hebrew says 'opposite Ginnesaret' (נגד גניסרת) — a geographic reference from the western shore's perspective. Greek TR has εἰς τὴν χώραν τῶν Γαδαρηνῶν ('to the region of the Gadarenes'). These are different place-naming systems: the Hebrew orients by relation to a known Galilean town; the Greek names the eastern region. A back-translator from Greek would write 'to the land of the Gadarenes,' not 'opposite Ginnesaret.'
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'opposite Ginnesaret.' Greek: 'the region of the Gadarenes/Gerasenes.' Entirely different geographic identification.

verses.translation: And immediately{H4116} when he went out{H3318} from the ship{H5600}, one{H259} man{H120} satan-possessed went out{H3318} to him on the way{H1870}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses מושטן (moshotan — 'satan-possessed'), from the root שטן (satan, H7854 — 'adversary'). Greek has δαιμονιζόμενος ('demonized'), from δαίμων. The Hebrew describes the condition through the OT adversary-theology of שטן (Job 1-2, Zechariah 3:1) — a prosecuting accuser in YHWH's court. Greek demonic cosmology derives from Hellenistic spirit-world categories entirely foreign to the OT. A back-translator from Greek would use a form from שד (shed — 'demon', Deut 32:17, Ps 106:37), NOT from שטן. This word appears throughout Mark 5 and is one of the most consistent one-way markers in the Hebrew Gospels.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'satan-possessed' (שטן-theology). Greek: 'demonized' (δαίμων-theology). Fundamentally different spiritual cosmologies.
Hebrew says the man came 'on the way' (בדרך). Greek says he came 'from the tombs' (ἐκ τῶν μνημείων). Different point of encounter.
translation_notes: 'Satan-possessed' for moshotan — preserving the שטן root. This is not equivalent to 'demonized'; it implies being under the power of the Adversary, the prosecuting angel of YHWH's court.

verses.translation: who dwelt{H7901} in the tombs{H6913}, and he was{H1961} so evil{H7451} that none were able{H3201} to hold{H2388} him with chains{H8333}.

greek_deviations: Hebrew says the man was 'evil' (רע) — a moral characterization. Greek describes his dwelling and binding without moral judgment. Different framing of the condition.
translation_notes: שוכב (shokhev) literally means 'lying/dwelling' — the word used for lying in bed, in a grave, or dwelling in a place. The man's habitation among tombs makes him ritually impure (Num 19:16).

verses.translation: Nor with irons{H1270}, for always{H8548} he broke{H7665} them, and they were not able{H3201} to quiet{H8252} him.

one_way_hebrew: Uses להשקיטו (lehashqito — 'to quiet him', from שקט H8252 — 'to be quiet/at rest'). This is the OT word for the land being at rest from war (Josh 11:23, 14:15, Judg 3:11,30, 5:31). Greek says δαμάσαι ('to tame/subdue'). A back-translator from Greek would use לכבוש (likhbosh — 'to subdue') or לרסן (to bridle), not the peace/rest verb שקט. The Hebrew implies the goal is peace and rest, not domination.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'to quiet him' (peace/rest). Greek: 'to tame him' (control/domination). Different objectives.

verses.translation: But he was{H1961} standing{H5975} in the night{H3915} and by day{H3117} in the tombs{H6913} and in the mountains{H2022}, crying out{H6817} and striking{H5221} himself with stones{H68}.

greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'standing' (עומד) in the tombs. Greek: 'cutting himself' (κατακόπτων). The Hebrew adds 'standing' as posture; both mention self-harm.
translation_notes: צועק (tso'eq, H6817) — the specific OT word for crying out in distress to God (Ex 2:23, 14:10, Judg 3:9). The man's shrieking is described with the same verb Israel uses when crying to YHWH for deliverance.

verses.translation: And when he saw{H7200} Yeshua from afar{H7350}, he came{H935} running{H4794} and prayed{H6419} to him.

one_way_hebrew: Uses והתפלל (ve-hitpallel — 'and he prayed', H6419). Greek has προσεκύνησεν ('worshipped/prostrated'). The Hebrew uses the hitpael of פלל — the specific verb for prayer in the OT (Gen 20:7, 1 Sam 1:10, 1 Kings 8:30, Dan 9:4). A back-translator from Greek would use השתחוה (hishtachaveh — 'bowed down/worshipped'), NOT the prayer verb. The Hebrew says the demoniac instinctively prayed to Yeshua — an extraordinary theological statement that even a satan-possessed man prays in the presence of the divine.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'prayed to him' (התפלל). Greek: 'worshipped him' (προσεκύνησεν). Prayer vs. prostration — different actions.

verses.translation: Saying in a high{H1364} voice{H6963}: What have you to do{H6213} with me, Yeshua, son{H1121} of the Most High{H5945} God{H433}? I adjure{H7650} you by the living{H2416} God{H410} that you not afflict me.

one_way_hebrew: Uses TWO different divine names in one verse: אלוה עליון (Eloah Elyon — 'God Most High', H433+H5945) and אל חי (El Chai — 'living God', H410+H2416). Greek uses θεός ('God') for both. A back-translator from Greek, seeing the same Greek word twice, would use the same Hebrew word both times. The Hebrew author distinguishes: Eloah (the singular poetic form, Job 3:4, 4:9) for the transcendent title, and El (the ancient Semitic divine name, Gen 14:18-22) for the oath formula. Two different names from two different OT traditions.

אל חי (El Chai — 'living God') is a specific OT oath formula: Joshua 3:10 ('by this you shall know that the living God is among you'), Psalm 42:3 ('my soul thirsts for God, for the living God'). The demon swears by this specific divine title. A back-translator from Greek τὸν θεόν would not independently reconstruct this OT oath formula.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: two different divine names (Eloah + El). Greek: θεός for both.
Hebrew: 'that you not afflict me' (תצערני). Greek: μή με βασανίσῃς ('do not torment me'). Hebrew צער is emotional distress; Greek βασανίζω is physical torture.
translation_notes: 'What have you to do with me' — a Hebrew idiom (מה לך...ממני) found in Judges 11:12, 2 Samuel 16:10, 2 Kings 3:13. The expression is native Hebrew, though Greek τί ἐμοὶ καὶ σοί is itself recognized as a Semitism.

verses.translation: And Yeshua said{H559} to him: Go out{H3318} outside{H2351}, spirit{H7307} not clean{H5355}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses רוח אינו נקי ('spirit not clean') — with נקי (naqi, H5355 — 'innocent/clean') rather than טמא (tameh — 'impure/unclean'). In the OT, נקי is a legal/moral term for innocence (Ex 23:7 'the innocent and righteous do not slay', Deut 19:10,13, 2 Kings 24:4). Greek has πνεῦμα τὸ ἀκάθαρτον ('the unclean spirit'). A back-translator from Greek ἀκάθαρτος would use טמא (the standard Levitical impurity word), NOT negate נקי. The Hebrew frames the spirit's condition as lack of moral innocence, not ritual impurity.
translation_notes: 'Not clean' rather than 'unclean' — preserving the Hebrew's distinctive negation structure (אינו נקי) rather than the single Greek word ἀκάθαρτον.

verses.translation: And he asked{H7592} him: What is your name{H8034}? And he answered{H6030}: My name{H8034} is Number{H4557}, for many{H7227} are they.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses מספר (mispar, H4557 — 'number/multitude'). Greek has Λεγιών (Legiōn — from Latin legio, a Roman military unit of ~5,000 soldiers). A back-translator from Greek would transliterate the Latin military term as לגיון, as Rabbinic literature commonly does (e.g., Midrash Rabbah). The Hebrew author uses a native Hebrew word, completely avoiding the Roman military loanword. This suggests the Hebrew author either (a) predates the Roman military presence that made 'Legion' a familiar term, or (b) deliberately chose a Hebrew equivalent. Either way, the direction Hebrew→Greek (translating mispar into the culturally resonant Latin term) is far more plausible than Greek→Hebrew.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: מספר ('Number/multitude'). Greek: Λεγιών ('Legion'). Entirely different names — native Hebrew vs. Latin military loanword.
translation_notes: 'Number' for mispar — the Hebrew word means both a count and a multitude (cf. Gen 34:30 'few in number'; 1 Chr 22:4 'without number'). The demon's name conveys 'we are a multitude' without Roman military imagery.

verses.translation: And he greatly{H3966} begged{H1245} him that he not drive him out{H1644} from that kingdom{H4438}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses מלכות (malkhut, H4438 — 'kingdom'). Greek has χώρα (chōra — 'region/country'). A back-translator from Greek would use ארץ (erets — 'land') or מדינה (medinah — 'province'), not the theologically loaded מלכות. The Hebrew word implies a domain of royal authority — the demon begs not to be expelled from a 'kingdom,' a concept with messianic overtones (Dan 2:44, 7:27). The demon recognizes it inhabits a domain of spiritual authority.

Uses יגרשהו (yegarsheihu — 'drive him out', H1644). This is the verb used for God driving Adam from Eden (Gen 3:24), driving out the Canaanite nations (Ex 23:28-31, Deut 33:27), and divorcing a wife (Lev 21:7). It carries connotations of permanent expulsion from a domain. Greek ἀποστείλῃ ('send away') is milder.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'kingdom' (מלכות). Greek: 'region' (χώρα). Different conceptual framework.
Hebrew: 'drive out' (גרש — permanent expulsion). Greek: 'send away' (ἀποστέλλω — dispatch).

verses.translation: And around{H5439} from there{H8033} many{H7227} swine{H2386} were grazing{H7462} [ ] [ ].

greek_deviations: Hebrew has lacunae (brackets [ ] [ ]) — text is damaged. Greek specifies πρὸς τῷ ὄρει ('near the mountain') and ἀγέλη χοίρων μεγάλη ('a great herd of swine'). The Hebrew damage may explain missing details.
translation_notes: חזירים (chazirim, H2386) — swine are the paradigmatic unclean animal in Torah law (Lev 11:7, Deut 14:8). Their presence signals Gentile territory.

verses.translation: And the spirits{H7307} entreated him, saying: Appoint us into the swine{H2386} so that we may enter{H935} them.

one_way_hebrew: Uses ונסוהו (ve-nisuhu — from נסה, H5254 — 'tested/tried him'). Greek has παρεκάλεσαν ('they begged'). The Hebrew root נסה is the word for testing/proving (Gen 22:1 God tested Abraham; Ex 15:25, 16:4 God tested Israel; Ex 17:2 Israel tested YHWH). A back-translator from Greek 'begged' would use בקש or חנן, not the testing verb. The Hebrew says the spirits tested Yeshua's authority — probing his power, not merely begging.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'tested/entreated him' (נסה). Greek: 'begged him' (παρακαλέω). Different relational dynamic.

verses.translation: And Yeshua consented{H3034} to them; immediately the satans{H7854} went out{H3318} and entered{H935} the swine{H2386}, and they cast{H5307} themselves into the sea{H3220} and were drowned — about two thousand{H505}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses השטנים (ha-satanim — 'the satans', PLURAL of שטן, H7854). Greek has τὰ πνεύματα τὰ ἀκάθαρτα ('the unclean spirits'). The Hebrew consistently uses שטן/שטנים (adversary/adversaries) terminology throughout this chapter, never שד/שדים (demon/demons). In the OT, שטן is a specific role in YHWH's court (Job 1-2, Zech 3:1, 1 Chr 21:1). The Hebrew author operates within OT adversary-theology; the Greek translator uses Hellenistic spirit-world categories. A back-translator from Greek would never independently replace δαιμόνια ('demons') with שטנים ('satans').

Uses הודהו (hodahu — from ידה, H3034 — 'acknowledged/consented'). The root ידה means both 'to confess/acknowledge' and 'to give thanks' (Gen 29:35, Ps 136). Greek has ἐπέτρεψεν ('permitted'). A back-translator would use הרשה (hirshah — 'permitted'), not the theologically weighted ידה.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'the satans' (שטנים). Greek: 'the unclean spirits.' Different terminology throughout.
Hebrew: the swine 'cast themselves' (reflexive). Greek: the herd 'rushed' (ὥρμησεν). The Hebrew emphasizes self-destruction.

verses.translation: And those who were keeping{H8104} them fled{H1272} and told{H5046} it in the city{H5892}, and all{H3605} went out{H3318} to see{H7200} what happened{H7136}.

greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'in the city' (singular). Greek: εἰς τὴν πόλιν καὶ εἰς τοὺς ἀγρούς ('into the city and into the fields'). Hebrew is more concise.

verses.translation: And when they came{H935} to Yeshua and saw{H7200} those who had formerly been satan-possessed, that they were in good{H2896} understanding{H7922}, they were afraid{H6342}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses בטוב שכלם (be-tov sikhlam — 'in good understanding/wisdom', H7922). Greek has σωφρονοῦντα ('being of sound mind'). The Hebrew שכל (sekhel) is a wisdom term — the same word used of David's skillful understanding (1 Sam 18:14,30), of the Maskil psalms, and of divine wisdom (Prov 12:8, 16:22). A back-translator from Greek σωφρονέω would use בדעת טובה ('in sound knowledge') or in a phrase with שפיות ('sanity'), not the wisdom-tradition term שכל.
translation_notes: 'Good understanding' for tov sikhlam — sekhel implies not merely sanity but wisdom and discernment. The healed man gained wisdom, not just mental stability.

verses.translation: And they recounted{H5608} what they saw{H7200}, and what was{H1961} the deed{H4639} of the one who was satan-possessed, and of the swine{H2386}.

translation_notes: מעשה (ma'aseh, H4639 — 'deed/work') — the standard OT word for God's works and mighty acts (Ps 8:7, 19:2, 92:5). The miracle is classified as a divine 'deed.'

verses.translation: And then they asked{H1245} him to depart{H6504} from their presence{H5227}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses מנוכחו (mi-nokhecho — 'from his/their presence', from נכח H5227). This word denotes being 'in front of/in the presence of' — used of standing before God (Prov 4:25, Lam 2:19). Greek has ἀπελθεῖν ἀπὸ τῶν ὁρίων ('depart from their borders'). A back-translator from 'borders' (ὁρίων) would use גבול (gevul — 'border'), not the presence-word נכח. The Hebrew frames the request as 'leave our presence' — a personal/spiritual expulsion, not geographic.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'from their presence' (relational). Greek: 'from their borders' (geographic).

verses.translation: And when Yeshua entered{H935} the ship{H5600}, the one who had formerly been satan-possessed began{H2490} to implore{H2603} him that he would go{H1980} with him.

one_way_hebrew: Uses להתחנן (lehithchanen — 'to implore grace', from חנן H2603 — 'to be gracious'). This is the hitpael of the root that gives us חן (chen — 'grace/favor'). Greek has παρεκάλει ('begged'). A back-translator from Greek would use בקש (biqesh — 'sought/asked'), not the grace-root verb. The Hebrew says the healed man 'sought grace' from Yeshua — the vocabulary of divine supplication (1 Kings 8:33, 2 Chr 6:24, Ps 30:9).

verses.translation: And Yeshua did not consent{H7521}, but said{H559} to him: Go{H1980} to your house{H1004} and to your own, and recount{H5608} the steadfast-love{H2617} that HaShem{H8034} did{H6213} for you.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses חסד (chesed, H2617 — 'steadfast-love/covenant-loyalty'). This is arguably the most theologically significant word in the entire OT — appearing 248 times, it denotes God's faithful covenant love (Ex 34:6, Ps 136:1-26 where each verse ends 'for his chesed endures forever'). Greek has ὅσα ὁ κύριός σοι πεποίηκεν καὶ ἠλέησέν σε ('how much the Lord has done for you and had mercy on you'). A back-translator from ἠλέησεν ('had mercy') would use רחמים (rachamim — 'mercy/compassion'), NOT the covenant-loyalty word chesed. The Hebrew identifies the healing as an act of covenant faithfulness, not merely mercy.

Uses השם (HaShem — 'the Name') for God. This is the distinctly Jewish circumlocution for YHWH, used to avoid pronouncing the divine name. Greek has κύριος (kyrios — 'Lord'). A back-translator from κύριος would use אדון (adon — 'lord') or write the tetragrammaton, NOT the rabbinic reverence-form השם.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'the steadfast-love' (חסד — one theological concept). Greek: 'how much... did... had mercy' (two separate verbs). The Hebrew condenses into a single covenant-theology term what Greek expresses as actions.
Hebrew: 'HaShem' (השם). Greek: κύριος ('Lord'). Different ways of referencing God.
translation_notes: 'Steadfast-love' for chesed — this translation attempts to capture both the steadfastness/faithfulness and the love dimensions. 'Mercy' or 'kindness' alone would lose the covenant dimension.
textual_notes: The chesed of YHWH as the content of testimony: the healed man is told to recount God's covenant-love, not merely the miracle itself. This parallels Psalm 107:1-2 — 'Give thanks to YHWH, for he is good, for his chesed endures forever. Let the redeemed of YHWH say so.'

verses.translation: And he went{H1980} proclaiming{H1875} the receiving of the steadfast-love{H2617} that HaShem{H8034} did{H6213} for him, and all{H3605} were amazed{H8539}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses דורש (doresh, H1875 — 'sought/expounded/proclaimed'). In the OT, דרש specifically means to seek God, inquire of a prophet, or expound Scripture (Ezra 7:10 'Ezra set his heart to darash the Torah of YHWH'; Ps 34:5, 105:4). Greek has κηρύσσειν ('to herald/proclaim'). A back-translator from Greek would use הכריז or קרא ('proclaim'), not the Torah-study verb דרש. The Hebrew says the man was 'expounding' — teaching and explaining — God's covenant-love.

בקבול החסד ('the receiving of the steadfast-love') — a unique Hebrew construction. The word קבול (receiving/acceptance) appears nowhere in Greek. The Greek simply says ὅσα ἐποίησεν ('how much he did'). The Hebrew adds the concept of actively receiving chesed — not merely being acted upon, but participating in covenant love.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'proclaiming/expounding the receiving of the steadfast-love.' Greek: 'proclaiming how much Jesus had done for him.' Entirely different content — covenant theology vs. miracle reporting.
Hebrew: 'HaShem.' Greek: ὁ Ἰησοῦς ('Jesus'). The Hebrew attributes the deed to God; the Greek to Jesus.
textual_notes: The Hebrew says the man proclaimed what HaShem (God) did. The Greek says he proclaimed what Jesus did. The Hebrew maintains the theological distinction between Yeshua as agent and HaShem as author of chesed.

verses.translation: And when Yeshua crossed{H5674} to the other side{H5676} of the sea{H3220} in a ship{H5600}, a great{H7227} multitude{H5971} gathered{H622} to him at the shore{H8193} of the sea{H3220}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses שפת הים (sfat ha-yam — 'the lip of the sea', H8193). שפה literally means 'lip' and is the Hebrew idiom for shoreline (Gen 22:17 'sand on the lip of the sea', Ex 14:30, Josh 11:4). Greek has παρὰ τὴν θάλασσαν ('beside the sea'). A back-translator from Greek would use יד הים (yad ha-yam — 'hand of the sea') or על הים ('by the sea'), not the poetic 'lip of the sea' idiom.
translation_notes: 'Shore' for sfat — literally 'lip.' The Hebrew idiom 'lip of the sea' is a vivid image preserved throughout the OT.

verses.translation: And there came{H935} to him one{H259} leader{H1419} from the house of assembly{H1004} by the name{H8034} of Yair{H2971}, and when he saw{H7200} him, he bowed{H3766} on his knees{H1290} at his feet{H7272}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses בית הכנסת (beit ha-knesset — 'house of assembly'). This is the native Hebrew term for a place of gathering. Greek has ἀρχισυναγώγων ('rulers of the synagogue'), using the Greek loanword συναγωγή. A back-translator from Greek would likely transliterate or use a calque of the Greek. The Hebrew preserves the pre-Greek native designation.

Uses כרע (kara, H3766 — 'bowed/knelt'). This is the specific OT word for kneeling in worship or submission — used of bowing before God (1 Kings 8:54, 2 Chr 6:13), of animals kneeling (Gen 49:9, Num 24:9), and of falling in death (Judg 5:27). Greek has πίπτει πρὸς τοὺς πόδας ('falls at the feet'). A back-translator from 'falls' (πίπτει) would use נפל (nafal — 'fell'), not the worship-posture verb כרע.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'a leader from the house of assembly.' Greek: 'one of the rulers of the synagogue.' Different institutional language.
Hebrew: 'bowed on his knees' (deliberate worship posture). Greek: 'fell at his feet' (collapse/prostration).
translation_notes: Yair (יאיר, H2971) — 'he enlightens,' from the root אור ('light'). This is an OT name: Jair the judge (Judg 10:3) and a Manassite clan leader (Num 32:41, Deut 3:14, 1 Chr 20:5).

verses.translation: Begging{H1245} and saying{H559}: My daughter{H1323} is near{H7138} to death{H4191}; come{H935} and lay{H5117} your hands{H3027} upon her that she may be healed{H7495}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses והנח (ve-hanach, from נוח H5117 — 'to rest/lay'). This is the root of Noah's name (Gen 5:29). The Hebrew says 'rest your hands upon her' — the laying-on of hands is described as an act of bestowing rest. Greek has ἐπιθῇς τὰς χεῖρας ('lay hands'). A back-translator would use שים (sim — 'put/place'), not the rest/Noah verb נוח.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'near to death' (קרובה למות). Greek: ἐσχάτως ἔχει ('is at an extreme/at the point of death'). The Hebrew is spatial ('near to'); the Greek is qualitative ('at the extreme').

verses.translation: And Yeshua went{H1980} with him, and a great{H7227} multitude followed{H1980} after{H310} him.
And a certain woman{H802} who had a flowing of blood{H1818} for twelve{H8147}{H6240} years{H8141} past{H5674}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses רפיון דם (rifyon dam — 'weakness/flowing of blood'). The word רפיון derives from רפה (raphah, H7503 — 'to be weak/slack'). This is a Hebrew medical term describing the condition as physical weakness/laxity. Greek has ἐν ῥύσει αἵματος ('in a flow of blood'). A back-translator from Greek ῥύσις ('flow') would use זוב (zov — 'discharge', the Levitical term from Lev 15:19-25) or שטף (shetef — 'flood/flow'), NOT the weakness/laxity term רפיון. The Hebrew frames the condition as bodily weakness; the Greek merely describes the discharge.
translation_notes: A woman with a blood flow is ritually impure under Leviticus 15:25 and renders impure anyone she touches. Her act of touching Yeshua's garment (v27) is an act of desperation that violates purity law.

verses.translation: And they spent{H3318} all{H3605} that she had on medicines{H7499}, to no benefit{H3276} that she found{H4672}.

greek_deviations: Hebrew is concise: 'spent all on medicines, to no benefit.' Greek expands: πολλὰ παθοῦσα ὑπὸ πολλῶν ἰατρῶν ('having suffered much under many physicians'). Hebrew omits physicians entirely, mentioning only medicines (רפואות).

verses.translation: And when she heard{H8085} that Yeshua Mashiach{H4899} came{H935} among{H996} the people{H5971}, she entered{H935} and touched{H5060} the back{H268} of his garments{H4403}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: The Hebrew says ישוע משיח (Yeshua Mashiach — 'Yeshua the Anointed One'). Greek has only τοῦ Ἰησοῦ ('about Jesus') without 'Christ/Anointed.' The title משיח (Mashiach, H4899) is the OT designation for the anointed king (1 Sam 2:10, Ps 2:2) and the anointed deliverer (Dan 9:25-26). A back-translator from Greek would NOT add a title absent from the source text. The Hebrew author includes it as the woman's understanding of who Yeshua is — the Mashiach.

Uses נגעה (nag'ah, H5060 — 'touched'). This is the specific OT verb for contact that transmits ritual impurity (Lev 5:2-3, 11:8, 15:19, Num 19:11). A woman in her condition who 'touches' (נגע) renders the touched person unclean. The Hebrew author uses the Levitical purity-law verb to underscore the audacity and faith of her act. Greek ἥψατο is more neutral.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'Yeshua Mashiach.' Greek: just 'Jesus.' The Messianic title is absent from Greek.
Hebrew: 'the back of his garments' (אחורי מלבושיו). Greek: τοῦ ἱματίου αὐτοῦ ('his garment'). Hebrew specifies 'behind' — she touched from the rear.

verses.translation: For she said{H559} within herself{H7130}: If I{H595} am able{H3201} to touch{H5060} his garment{H3830}, I shall be healed{H7495}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses אנכי (anokhi, H595) — the archaic/solemn first-person pronoun, then switches to אני (ani, H589) in the same verse. אנכי is the form used in the Ten Commandments (אנכי יהוה אלהיך, Ex 20:2) and in solemn divine/prophetic declarations (Gen 15:1, Ex 3:6). Greek has no equivalent distinction between pronoun registers. A back-translator would use the common אני throughout. The deliberate use of אנכי for the conditional oath ('if I am able') and אני for the result ('I shall be healed') marks the first clause as a solemn vow.

Uses בקרבה (be-qirbah — 'in her midst/inner being', from קרב H7130). This is the OT word for the interior of a person or the midst of Israel where God dwells (Ex 34:9, Num 14:14, Deut 23:15). Greek has ἐν ἑαυτῇ ('in herself'). The Hebrew carries the theological weight of 'in her innermost being' — the place where God's presence dwells.
translation_notes: 'Within herself' for be-qirbah — preserving the depth of the Hebrew, which implies more than inner thought; it implies the core of her being.

verses.translation: And immediately the flowing of the blood{H1818} stopped, and she felt{H7275} that she was healed{H7495}.

greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'the flowing of the blood stopped' (passive — the flow ceased). Greek: ἐξηράνθη ἡ πηγὴ τοῦ αἵματος ('the fountain of the blood was dried up'). Different metaphor: Hebrew uses stoppage; Greek uses drying of a spring.
translation_notes: הגרת (ha-geret) — 'the flowing,' possibly from גרר (to drag/flow) or גרה (to provoke/stir). A rare Hebrew medical term for chronic blood flow.

verses.translation: And Yeshua, who knew{H3045} in himself the truth{H571} that from him [power] went out{H3318}, turned{H2015} toward the people{H5971} and said{H559}: Who touched{H5060} my garment{H3830}?

one_way_hebrew: Hebrew says Yeshua knew 'the truth' (האמת, emet, H571) that from him [power] went out. Greek says ἐπιγνοὺς τὴν ἐξ αὐτοῦ δύναμιν ἐξελθοῦσαν ('perceiving the power going out from him'). The Hebrew substitutes 'truth' (אמת) for Greek 'power' (δύναμις/כח). A back-translator from Greek would write הכח (ha-koach — 'the power'), not האמת ('the truth'). The Hebrew frames Yeshua's awareness as knowledge of truth rather than perception of power — an epistemological rather than phenomenological description.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'the truth that from him went out.' Greek: 'the power going out from him.' Truth vs. power.
Hebrew omits the word for 'power' entirely.
translation_notes: [Power] added in brackets to clarify what went out — the Hebrew leaves this implicit, saying only 'from him went out.'

verses.translation: And his disciples said{H559} to him: You see{H7200} that your people{H5971} press{H1849} you, and you say{H559}: Who touched{H5060} me?

one_way_hebrew: Uses עמך (amkha — 'your people'). The Hebrew says 'your people press you' — implying that the crowd belongs to Yeshua, that they are 'his people.' Greek has ὁ ὄχλος ('the crowd'). A back-translator from 'the crowd' would write ההמון or העם without the possessive. The Hebrew possessive 'your people' echoes God's relationship with Israel — 'my people' (עמי) throughout the prophets.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'your people' (possessive — relational). Greek: 'the crowd' (neutral).

verses.translation: And he looked around{H5027} to see{H7200} if he could find the one who did{H6213} this.

And the woman{H802}, afraid{H6342} and trembling{H3373}, knowing{H3045} well the wonder{H6382} that was done{H6213} in her, knelt{H1288} before him{H6440} and told{H559} him all{H3605} the truth{H571}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses הפלא (ha-pele, H6382 — 'the wonder'). This is the OT's specific word for divine wonder-working — the wonders of the Exodus (Ex 15:11 'doing wonders'), the wonders God performs (Ps 77:12,15, 78:12), and the prophetic 'Wonderful Counselor' title (Isa 9:5). Greek has no single equivalent here. A back-translator from Greek would not independently select the loaded OT term פלא.

Uses ונברכה (ve-nivrekhah — 'and she knelt/blessed', from ברך H1288). The root ברך means both 'to kneel' and 'to bless.' The woman simultaneously knelt and invoked blessing. Greek has προσέπεσεν ('fell before'). A back-translator would use נפלה (naflah — 'fell'), not the blessing/kneeling verb ברך.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'the wonder done in her' (פלא). Greek: no equivalent noun — only implies it through context.

verses.translation: And he understood{H995} and said{H559} to her: My daughter{H1323}, your faith{H530} has saved{H3467} you; go{H1980} in peace{H7965} and be healed{H7495}.

one_way_hebrew: Hebrew adds הבין (hevin, H995 — 'he understood/discerned') before speaking. This is absent in Greek. The verb בין is the OT wisdom verb for discernment (Prov 1:2, Dan 9:2, Neh 8:8). The Hebrew shows Yeshua exercising prophetic discernment before pronouncing the healing.

Uses הושיעך (hoshi'akh — 'has saved you', from ישע, H3467). This is the root of the name ישוע (Yeshua). The wordplay only works in Hebrew: 'Yeshua says your faith has yeshua'd (saved) you.' Greek σέσωκεν (from σῴζω) does not carry this nominal wordplay. This Hebraic pun on the Savior's own name is a strong one-way marker.
greek_deviations: Hebrew adds 'he understood' (הבין) — absent from Greek.
translation_notes: 'Saved' for hoshi'akh rather than 'healed' — to preserve the wordplay with Yeshua's name and the full scope of ישע (which includes both physical and spiritual deliverance).
textual_notes: The name ישוע (Yeshua) literally means 'he saves' — from the root ישע (yasha, H3467). When Yeshua says 'your faith has saved you,' the Hebrew audience hears the name and the verb as one: 'Yeshua (Salvation) says your faith has yeshua'd (saved) you.'

verses.translation: And while he was speaking{H1696}, they came{H935} to the deputy{H5461} of the house of assembly{H1004} and said{H559} to him: Your daughter{H1323} has died{H4191}; why do you trouble yourself today{H3117} still{H5750}?

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses סגן (segan, H5461 — 'deputy/officer'). This is the priestly/Temple administrative title used in Nehemiah 2:16, 4:8, 5:7, 7:5, Jeremiah 51:23,28,57. In Second Temple literature, the סגן הכהנים was the Temple captain, second only to the High Priest. Greek has ἀρχισυνάγωγος ('ruler of the synagogue'). A back-translator from Greek would use ראש בית הכנסת ('head of the synagogue') or translate ἀρχι- as שר ('officer'), NOT reach for the Temple administrative term סגן. The Hebrew author sees the local assembly leader through Temple-priestly institutional categories.

Hebrew: 'why do you trouble yourself today still' (מצטער...היום עוד). Greek: τί ἔτι σκύλλεις τὸν διδάσκαλον ('why do you still trouble the teacher?'). The Hebrew says the father troubles himself; the Greek says he troubles the teacher. Completely different objects. Also, Hebrew adds 'today' (היום) which is absent from Greek.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'trouble yourself.' Greek: 'trouble the teacher.' Different objects.
Hebrew: adds 'today' (היום). Greek: absent.
Hebrew: 'deputy' (סגן). Greek: 'ruler of the synagogue' (ἀρχισυνάγωγος). Different titles.
translation_notes: 'Deputy' for segan — preserving the Temple administrative connotation. This is not merely a 'ruler' but a specific rank in the priestly hierarchy.

verses.translation: And the teacher{H3925} Yeshua, who heard{H8085} this, said{H559}: Do not fear{H6342}; only have good{H2896} faith{H530} in HaShem{H8034}, and believe{H539}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses המלמד (ha-melamed, H3925 — 'the teacher'). From למד (lamed — 'to learn/teach'). This is a specifically Jewish educational title — the same root gives us תלמוד (Talmud — 'learning') and תלמיד (talmid — 'student'). Greek has no title here; it simply says ὁ Ἰησοῦς ('Jesus'). A back-translator from Greek would not add a title absent from the source.

Hebrew: 'good faith in HaShem' (טובה אמונה בשם). Greek: μόνον πίστευε ('only believe'). The Hebrew specifies the object of faith — HaShem (God) — while the Greek leaves faith objectless. Additionally, the Hebrew qualifies the faith as 'good' (טובה), absent in Greek. A back-translator from Greek would write האמן בלבד ('only believe'), not independently add 'good faith in HaShem.'
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'the teacher Yeshua.' Greek: just 'Jesus.'
Hebrew: 'good faith in HaShem.' Greek: 'only believe.' Different scope and object of faith.

verses.translation: And he did not take any man{H120} with him except Keyfa and Yaaqov{H3290}.

greek_deviations: Hebrew: only Keyfa and Yaaqov (two disciples). Greek adds Ἰωάννην τὸν ἀδελφὸν Ἰακώβου ('John the brother of James'), making three. The Hebrew is shorter.
translation_notes: כיפא (Keyfa) — Aramaic for 'rock,' the Hebrew equivalent of Peter. The Hebrew text preserves the Semitic form, not the Greek Πέτρος.

verses.translation: And they came{H935} to the house{H1004} of the deputy{H5461} of the house of assembly, and saw{H7200} there much{H3966} weeping{H1065} and outcries{H6818}.

translation_notes: צעקות (tse'aqot, H6818) — 'outcries,' the same word used for Israel's cry under Egyptian oppression (Ex 3:7,9). The mourning cries are described with Exodus-deliverance language.

verses.translation: And Yeshua entered{H935} the house{H1004} and said{H559}: Why are you troubled{H943} and weeping{H1058}? The girl{H5291} — is she dead{H4191}? Rather, she is sleeping{H3463}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses נבוכים (nevukhim, H943 — 'troubled/confused'). This echoes Exodus 14:3 where Pharaoh says the Israelites are נבכים (entangled/confused) in the land. Greek has θορυβεῖσθε ('make commotion/uproar'). A back-translator from Greek would use סוערים (stormy/riotous) or המונים (noisy), not the Exodus-specific bewilderment verb.
greek_deviations: Hebrew structures Yeshua's statement as a question: 'The girl — is she dead?' (with interrogative האם). Greek is declarative: 'the child has not died.' Different rhetorical form.

verses.translation: And all{H3605} mocked{H3932} him. And Yeshua drove{H1644} them all outside{H2351}, except the father{H1} and the mother{H517} and the disciples who were with him, and they entered{H935} the place{H4725} where the girl{H5291} lay{H7901}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses גרש (garash, H1644 — 'drove out'). This is the verb used for God driving Adam from Eden (Gen 3:24), driving out the Canaanite nations (Ex 23:28-31, Deut 33:27), and Hagar being driven out (Gen 21:10). It implies forceful, authoritative expulsion. Greek has ἐκβαλών ('casting out') which is strong but lacks the specific OT exile connotation.

verses.translation: And he took{H3947} her by the hand{H3027} and said{H559} to her: Talitha Qumi{H6965} — which means: Virgin{H1330}, I say{H559} to you, arise{H6965}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: The Hebrew glosses טליתא (Talitha) as בתולה (betulah, H1330 — 'virgin'). Greek glosses it as κοράσιον ('little girl'). The Hebrew author interprets the Aramaic word through the lens of virginal purity — specifically the word used in Isaiah 7:14 (הנה הבתולה הרה — 'behold, the virgin is with child'). A back-translator from Greek κοράσιον would use נערה (na'arah — 'girl') or ילדה (yaldah — 'child'), NEVER בתולה. The Hebrew interpretation loads the resurrection of this twelve-year-old girl with Isaiah's virgin prophecy. The girl is restored in her virginal wholeness — a sign pointing to resurrection itself.

The Aramaic טליתא קומי is preserved in brackets as a foreign phrase, then explained in Hebrew. This is the same authorial practice seen in Revelation where foreign words are marked בלעז ('in a foreign tongue'). A Hebrew author explains Aramaic for Hebrew readers; a Greek author would not need to explain what is already rendered in Greek.
greek_deviations: Hebrew gloss of Talitha: בתולה ('virgin'). Greek gloss: κοράσιον ('little girl'). Fundamentally different interpretations of the Aramaic.
Hebrew preserves Aramaic in brackets and provides a Hebrew explanation. Greek transliterates the Aramaic and provides a Greek translation.
translation_notes: 'Virgin' for betulah — this is not merely 'girl' but carries the full weight of virginal purity. The twelve-year-old girl is at the age of betrothal, and betulah specifically denotes an unmarried young woman of intact purity.
textual_notes: Talitha (טליתא) is Aramaic feminine for 'young girl/lamb.' The Hebrew author's choice to gloss this as betulah rather than na'arah reveals a theological interpretation: the girl raised from death is a 'virgin' — a sign of innocence restored, death's power over the pure overturned.

verses.translation: And immediately the girl{H5291} returned alive{H2416} and walked{H1980}; she had been twelve{H8147}{H6240} years{H8141}. And all{H3605} were astonished{H926} at the greatness{H1433} of the wonder{H6382}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses מגודל הפלא (mi-godel ha-pele — 'at the greatness of the wonder'). This is a constructed Hebrew expression combining גודל (H1433 — 'greatness', as in Deut 3:24, 5:24, 9:26, 11:2) with פלא (H6382 — 'wonder'). Greek has ἐξέστησαν ἐκστάσει μεγάλῃ ('they were amazed with great amazement') — a cognate accusative construction. A back-translator from Greek would write תמהו תמיהה גדולה ('amazed with great amazement'), not independently construct 'the greatness of the wonder.'
translation_notes: The girl was twelve years old — the same duration as the woman's blood flow (v25). This numerical parallel connects the two miracles: twelve years of death-in-life (the woman) and twelve years of life-unto-death (the girl).

verses.translation: And he commanded{H6680} them that they should not tell{H559} it, and afterward commanded{H6680} that they give{H5414} her to eat{H398}.

chapter_notes.summary: Mark 5 in Hebrew contains at least 15 strong one-way translation markers. The most striking: (1) מושטן/שטנים ('satan-possessed/satans') throughout — the Hebrew uses OT adversary-theology (שטן from Job 1-2, Zech 3:1) while Greek uses Hellenistic demonic categories (δαιμονιζόμενος), and no back-translator would replace 'demons' with 'satans'; (2) מספר ('Number') instead of 'Legion' — avoiding the Latin military loanword entirely; (3) חסד ('steadfast-love') instead of 'mercy' — the covenant-loyalty word appearing 248 times in the OT; (4) סגן ('deputy') for the assembly leader — a Temple administrative term from Nehemiah and Jeremiah; (5) טליתא glossed as בתולה ('virgin') not 'little girl' — connecting to Isaiah 7:14; (6) השם ('HaShem') for God — the rabbinic circumlocution; (7) משיח added to Yeshua's name where Greek lacks it; (8) הושיעך ('has saved you') creating a wordplay on Yeshua's own name (ישוע/ישע) that only works in Hebrew; (9) אנכי (archaic first person) in the woman's oath; (10) Two different divine names (אלוה/אל) in v7 where Greek has θεός for both. The chapter also shows consistent Hebrew theological framing: truth over power (v30), covenant-love over mercy (v19), and virginal purity over girlhood (v41).
